brief.context: Scale plastic modeling for a complete beginner getting into it as a hobby: kits, tools, techniques, community, history.
brief.subject: Scale plastic modeling
brief.scope: Kits, tools, paints, techniques, scales, history, community and workspace basics
brief.purpose: Give a beginner a map for starting the hobby

node.label: Plastic modeling
node.summary: Scale plastic modeling is the hobby of assembling and painting miniature replicas of aircraft, vehicles, ships and figures from kits.
node.hook: Turn plastic parts on a frame into a tiny, convincing replica.

node.label: Kits
node.summary: A plastic kit is a set of injection-molded parts on runners (sprues) that you cut, clean, glue and paint into a miniature replica.
node.hook: The box you buy decides how your first month goes.

node.label: Tools
node.summary: A small kit of cutters, knives, files and glue covers nearly every beginner build.
node.hook: You need fewer tools than the hobby shop wants you to think.

node.label: Paints & Finishing
node.summary: Painting and finishing give a model color, depth and a protective surface.
node.hook: Paint is where a gray plastic copy becomes a miniature.

node.label: Techniques
node.summary: Core building and painting methods learned step by step.
node.hook: The skills that make a model look finished.

node.label: Scales & Subjects
node.summary: Scale is the size ratio of the model to the real thing; subject is what it depicts.
node.hook: Pick a scale, then a subject, and the rest follows.

node.label: History
node.summary: The hobby grew from wooden and metal models into mass-produced plastic kits after WWII.
node.hook: Plastic modeling is older than most people expect.

node.label: Community
node.summary: Clubs, forums and shows are where beginners learn fastest.
node.hook: You do not have to learn alone.

node.label: Workspace & Safety
node.summary: Good lighting, ventilation and organization make building safe and enjoyable.
node.hook: A little setup prevents most hobby disasters.

node.label: Injection-molded kits
node.summary: Styrene parts are molded on runners; the standard format for cars, planes, ships and armor.
node.hook: Most kits are plastic parts you snip off a frame.

node.label: Snap-fit kits
node.summary: Parts click together with pegs and sockets; often marketed as easy or starter kits with color-molded plastic.
node.hook: No glue needed, so they are the friendliest place to start.

node.label: Resin and 3D-printed kits
node.summary: Small-batch casts or prints used for rare subjects and upgrades; they need washing, curing and different glue.
node.hook: Fine detail, but fragile and fiddly for beginners.

node.label: Gunpla
node.summary: Plastic kits of Gundam mecha, known for color-separated parts and articulated joints.
node.hook: Bandai robot kits that snap together and look amazing.

node.label: HG
node.summary: High Grade kits are 1/144 scale, simple to build and the usual first Gunpla.
node.hook: The cheap, quick entry grade for Gundam kits.

node.label: MG
node.summary: Master Grade kits are typically 1/100 with inner frames and finer articulation.
node.hook: More parts, more detail, more hours.

node.label: Beginner-friendly brands
node.summary: Tamiya, Revell, Airfix and Bandai are widely recommended for good fit and clear instructions.
node.hook: Some makers just fit better than others.

node.label: Tamiya
node.summary: Japanese maker known for precise molds and excellent paint range; good for armor, cars and aircraft.
node.hook: The gold standard for fit and instructions.

node.label: Airfix
node.summary: Long-running maker of aircraft and ships, with affordable starter sets that include paint and glue.
node.hook: British classic that has hooked generations.

node.label: Reading the instructions
node.summary: Instruction sheets show part numbers, paint call-outs and assembly order; test-fit before gluing.
node.hook: Dry-fit first and the instructions become your friend.

node.label: Cutting tools
node.summary: Tools for removing parts from sprues and trimming flash and seams.
node.hook: Clean cuts mean less cleanup later.

node.label: Sprue nippers
node.summary: Side cutters with a flat edge that snip parts off runners cleanly, leaving minimal nub.
node.hook: The single best tool upgrade you can buy.

node.label: Hobby knife
node.summary: A pen-style knife with replaceable blades for trimming, scraping seam lines and cutting masking tape.
node.hook: A sharp blade does the precise work.

node.label: Adhesives
node.summary: Different glues suit different jobs; plastic cement bonds styrene, while CA and PVA handle other materials.
node.hook: The right glue welds plastic instead of just sticking it.

node.label: Plastic cement
node.summary: Solvent glue that softens styrene so two parts fuse; applied with a brush or thin liquid versions that flow into joints.
node.hook: It melts the surfaces together into one solid piece.

node.label: CA glue
node.summary: Cyanoacrylate (super glue) bonds almost anything fast but can fog clear parts and is hard to reposition.
node.hook: Instant bond for resin, metal and quick fixes.

node.label: PVA glue
node.summary: Water-based glue that dries clear; used for canopies and windows because it will not fog the plastic.
node.hook: White craft glue that is perfect for clear parts.

node.label: Sanding and filing
node.summary: Files, sanding sticks and sponges remove seams, nubs and mold lines.
node.hook: Smooth surfaces are what separate good builds from great ones.

node.label: Sanding sticks
node.summary: Foam-backed sticks in various grits for smoothing seams and flat areas.
node.hook: Flat, flexible and cheap.

node.label: Grit progression
node.summary: Start around 400 grit to remove seams and finish near 1000 or higher before painting.
node.hook: Go from rough to fine, never skip steps.

node.label: Holding and measuring
node.summary: Tweezers, clamps and cutting mats make small parts manageable.
node.hook: Third hands and tweezers save sanity.

node.label: Tweezers
node.summary: Fine-tip and angled tweezers for placing decals and small details.
node.hook: Tiny parts will launch themselves without them.

node.label: Cutting mat
node.summary: A self-healing mat gives a safe, non-slip surface for trimming and cutting.
node.hook: Protects your table and your blades.

node.label: Putty and filler
node.summary: Modeling putty fills seams and sink marks; it is sanded flush once cured.
node.hook: Fills the gaps the factory left.

text: Glue choice is the quiet hinge: plastic cement, CA and PVA each solve a different problem.

node.label: Acrylic paint
node.summary: Acrylics such as Tamiya and Vallejo are easy to clean and good for brushing and airbrushing.
node.hook: Water-based, low-odor, beginner-safe.

node.label: Enamel paint
node.summary: Solvent-based paint such as Humbrol offers durable coverage but needs ventilation and thinner for cleanup.
node.hook: Tough and classic, but smells and takes longer to dry.

node.label: Lacquer paint
node.summary: Strong-solvent paints popular for airbrushing, giving smooth thin coats and fast layering.
node.hook: Dries fast and sprays beautifully.

node.label: Primer
node.summary: A thin first coat that grips the plastic, reveals flaws and gives paint an even base.
node.hook: The step that makes paint actually stick.

node.label: Clear coats
node.summary: Protective top coats that seal decals and weathering and set the sheen.
node.hook: Gloss, satin or matte decides the final look.

node.label: Gloss coat
node.summary: Glossy clear layer applied before decals so they settle without silvering.
node.hook: Smooth base that decals love.

node.label: Matte coat
node.summary: Flat finish applied last to make a model look scale-realistic.
node.hook: Kills the toy-like shine.

node.label: Brushes
node.summary: Round brushes in sizes 0 to 2 cover most detail and base painting.
node.hook: A few good brushes beat a dozen cheap ones.

node.label: Airbrushing
node.summary: A tool that sprays thin paint with compressed air for gradients and large areas.
node.hook: The upgrade that gives smooth, even coats.

node.label: Test fitting
node.summary: Checking that parts align before gluing prevents gaps and ruined seams.
node.hook: Dry-fit everything before you commit glue.

node.label: Seam removal
node.summary: Glue, sand and re-detail the seam so a model looks molded as one piece.
node.hook: Hide the line where two halves meet.

node.label: Masking
node.summary: Applying low-tack tape or liquid mask to protect areas during painting.
node.hook: Crisp edges come from good tape.

node.label: Masking tape
node.summary: Specialist tape like Tamiya tape gives sharp lines without lifting paint.
node.hook: Thin hobby tape follows curves.

node.label: Decals
node.summary: Printed decals are soaked, slid into place and sealed with a clear coat.
node.hook: Waterslide transfers add markings and realism.

node.label: Decal setting solution
node.summary: Chemicals that soften decals so they conform to curved or detailed surfaces.
node.hook: Helps decals melt into panel lines.

node.label: Weathering
node.summary: Washes, drybrushing and pigments add age, grime and battle damage.
node.hook: Dirt and wear turn a toy into a story.

node.label: Panel line wash
node.summary: Thinned paint flowed into recesses to emphasize panel lines.
node.hook: Dark thin paint that brings out the detail.

node.label: Drybrushing
node.summary: Dragging a nearly dry brush over detail to catch edges with lighter color.
node.hook: Highlights raised edges with almost no paint.

node.label: Airbrush basics
node.summary: Learning to thin paint, control pressure and clean the airbrush.
node.hook: Thin paint, low pressure, patience.

node.label: 1:72 scale
node.summary: A popular aircraft scale offering many subjects in modest size.
node.hook: Small and shelf-friendly, common for aircraft.

node.label: 1:48 scale
node.summary: Larger than 1/72 with more detail room, common for fighters and WWII planes.
node.hook: The Goldilocks aircraft scale.

node.label: 1:35 scale
node.summary: Dominant scale for tanks and soldiers with huge aftermarket support.
node.hook: The standard for military armor and figures.

node.label: 1:24 scale
node.summary: Common scale for car kits, with detailed engines and interiors.
node.hook: Big enough to see every cable in a car engine.

node.label: Aircraft
node.summary: Aircraft kits teach careful assembly and painting of curved surfaces.
node.hook: Wings, canopies and tricky camouflage.

node.label: Armor
node.summary: Military vehicles reward painting and weathering skill.
node.hook: Tanks teach weathering better than anything.

node.label: Cars and motorcycles
node.summary: Automotive subjects emphasize smooth paint and detailed assemblies.
node.hook: Gloss paint, chrome and tiny engines.

node.label: Ships
node.summary: Naval models range from simple hulls to intricate rigging.
node.hook: Rigging, hulls and plenty of patience.

node.label: Sci-fi and fantasy
node.summary: Fictional subjects give freedom in color schemes and weathering.
node.hook: Starships, mecha and made-up worlds.

node.label: Early scale models
node.summary: Before plastics, hobbyists carved wooden solids and built metal kits.
node.hook: Wood and metal came first.

node.label: Postwar plastic boom
node.summary: In the 1950s companies like Airfix and Revell mass-produced affordable plastic kits.
node.hook: Injection molding made kits cheap.

node.label: Japanese precision era
node.summary: From the 1960s Japanese makers set new standards for fit and engineering.
node.hook: Tamiya and Hasegawa raised the bar.

node.label: Rise of Gunpla
node.summary: Bandai launched Gundam kits in 1980 and made snap-fit modeling mainstream.
node.hook: A TV robot show became a model empire.

node.label: Modern era
node.summary: Kits now use CAD design, multi-color molding and printed aftermarket parts.
node.hook: Computer-designed kits and 3D printing.

node.label: Local clubs (IPMS)
node.summary: IPMS chapters host build nights, contests and swap meets.
node.hook: In-person tips and friendly critique.

node.label: Online forums
node.summary: Sites like Scale Model Forums and Reddit host thousands of build threads.
node.hook: Build logs and answers to any question.

node.label: YouTube tutorials
node.summary: Video channels demonstrate painting and assembly techniques step by step.
node.hook: Watch someone else make the mistakes first.

node.label: Contests and shows
node.summary: Competitions display models and give judges feedback to builders.
node.hook: See what is possible and get feedback.

node.label: Hobby shops
node.summary: Local stores offer advice and supplies and often host events.
node.hook: Where you can touch the boxes.

node.label: Ventilation
node.summary: Work with airflow or a spray booth, especially with enamel and lacquer.
node.hook: Paint fumes are not a joke.

node.label: Lighting
node.summary: Bright, daylight-balanced lamps reduce eye strain and reveal flaws.
node.hook: You cannot fix what you cannot see.

node.label: Knife safety
node.summary: Blades are sharp; keep fingers clear and use a mat.
node.hook: Cut away from your fingers.

node.label: Storage and display
node.summary: Cases and shelves keep finished models safe and organized.
node.hook: Dust is the long-term enemy.

node.label: Budget planning
node.summary: A starter set of tools and a couple of paints costs far less than a full workshop.
node.hook: Start with one kit and the basics.

edge.why: Injection-molded styrene kits are assembled with solvent cement.
Clear parts and decals need glues that do not fog or damage the surface.
Resin does not melt with plastic cement, so CA glue is used.
Clean cuts leave less to sand away.
Sanding is a core step in removing seams.
Filler closes gaps before sanding.
Primer reveals flaws and sets the base for masking.
Decals sit best on a gloss surface.
A final matte coat seals weathering effects.
The tool and the skill of using it.
Strong solvents demand good airflow.
Enamel fumes need ventilation.
Gunpla is the product of that history.
Tamiya led the precision era.
Airfix was a pioneer of the postwar boom.
Armor is most commonly built in 1/35.
Fighters and WWII planes often come in 1/48.
Video is the easiest way to learn weathering.
Clubs host and prepare builders for contests.
Good light reveals gaps during dry-fit.

text: Painting skill compounds: primer, masking, decals and clear coats all depend on each other.
